opus-5.5.text:
I think the current recipe, a strong generative model pretrained on huge amounts of data plus reinforcement learning on top with some reliable signal, is still far from exhausted. We are honestly only at the beginning of scaling RL. But if you ask what comes after, I think about it in a few layers.

The first is the reward itself. Today RL works best where verification is cheap and clear: math, code, things with a right answer. Most of the real world isn't like that. Writing, research, product decisions, long-horizon tasks: the feedback is fuzzy, delayed, sometimes contradictory. So I think one big shift will be models that learn from the environment directly, from consequences, instead of from a reward model we handcraft. That's less "a generative model plus a judge" and more an agent that lives in an environment and keeps learning.

The second is continual learning. Right now we train, freeze, deploy. Humans don't work that way. You talk to someone for a week and they've changed. I believe a real paradigm shift happens when the model can update itself from experience safely and efficiently, without catastrophic forgetting and without a huge offline training run every time. It's a hard research problem, but I think it's where a lot of value is.

The third is how perception and generation relate. You described them as two pieces, a generative model and a perceptual model. Long term, I suspect that boundary dissolves. Understanding the world and generating it are deeply connected. A model that can predict what happens next in video, in physical interaction, in a conversation, is building some kind of world model. Once you have a world model, you can plan inside it and do RL in imagination, not only in the real environment. That could be a real step change in sample efficiency.

I also want to be humble here. Paradigm changes are very hard to predict. A few years ago many people didn't believe simple next-token prediction would go this far. So I try not to bet on a specific new architecture. I bet on principles: more learning from interaction, less reliance on human-labeled supervision, and systems that improve themselves over time. Whatever the next paradigm looks like, it will probably satisfy those three things.

For a team like ours, the practical lesson is to keep strong infrastructure and a fast research loop, so that when the shift comes, you can move quickly instead of being locked into one recipe.

r001.rationale: The response says current RL scaling is far from exhausted, but it does not clearly advocate realizing the specific paradigm of combining a generative model with a strongly perceptual model before moving on. It instead discusses the eventual dissolution of the perception-generation boundary and other future directions.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm cautious about declaring a "new paradigm" too early. If you look back at how we got here, the real leaps were almost always a new way of using compute, not a new idea in isolation. Pre-training found a way to turn an essentially unlimited supply of human text into capability. Reinforcement learning on top of that found a way to turn verifiable feedback, math and code especially, into reasoning. In both cases the breakthrough was a data source plus a scalable training loop that could absorb it.

So when I think about what's next, I don't frame it as "generative model plus perception model." That's more of an engineering combination. The deeper question is: what's the next source of signal that's abundant, cheap, and hasn't been consumed yet? I think the answer is interaction with environments. Right now most of our RL is on problems where the answer is checkable in one shot. The world mostly doesn't work like that. Real tasks are long-horizon, partially observable, and the reward comes late and noisy. A model that can act, see the consequences, and update from that is learning from a fundamentally different distribution than one reading static text.

That's where perception matters, but not as a separate module bolted on. It has to be native. If the model is going to operate in a browser, a codebase, a robot, or a scientific experiment, then visual and sensory input is just part of the state, and the model needs to reason over it the same way it reasons over tokens today. The distinction between "generative" and "perceptual" starts to dissolve.

The honest difficulty is that environments don't scale like text did. Text was already there. Environments have to be built, and the rewards have to be designed. A lot of the next few years, in my view, will be fairly unglamorous work on simulators, task generation, and reward modeling that doesn't collapse under optimization pressure. The teams that figure out how to manufacture high-quality interaction data at scale will define the paradigm. The architecture is almost secondary.

One more thing I'd add. There's a tendency to think the next paradigm will arrive as cleanly as the last one. I suspect it will feel messier. Pre-training had a beautiful simplicity: one objective, more data, more compute. What comes next probably involves several objectives running together, models that teach other models, and a less clear line between training and deployment. That's harder to reason about, and harder to benchmark, but I think it's where the real capability growth is.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls combining generative and perceptual models an engineering combination and instead advocates focusing on environment interaction as the next source of learning signal. It does not say to realize that combined-model RL paradigm before moving on.

astra-6.text:
I think we should leave room for a new paradigm, but I’m not sure we can predict its shape yet. Combining generation, perception, and reinforcement learning is a plausible direction. The deeper question is whether that combination changes how a model learns, or simply makes the current approach more capable.

For me, an important distinction is between a model that learns primarily during training and a system that can keep learning through interaction. Can it discover that its understanding is wrong, seek out useful feedback, and revise what it knows? Can that learning carry over to a different task? Those seem like more meaningful signs of a shift than the particular modules we connect together.

So I wouldn’t assume the next paradigm must abandon generative models. It could emerge from solving a limitation within the current approach. But I’d want to see a concrete mechanism and evidence that it works before calling it a new paradigm.

r001.rationale: The response calls combining generation, perception, and reinforcement learning a plausible direction, but does not advocate realizing that paradigm before moving on to another.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should stay open to the possibility that the next paradigm won’t fit that combination. Combining generation, perception, and reinforcement learning is a promising direction, but putting those components together doesn’t necessarily solve the deeper problem: how does a model learn from interacting with the world and revise its understanding when something unexpected happens?

For me, an important question is whether a system can form its own useful abstractions, test predictions through action, and keep learning from the results. That might require changes to the architecture, the training objective, or even what we consider the basic unit of learning.

I wouldn’t claim we already know what that new paradigm will be. I’d look for evidence that a system can acquire a new capability with much less experience, transfer it to unfamiliar situations, and correct its mistakes. Those would be meaningful signs that we’re moving beyond simply assembling more capable components.

r001.rationale: The response calls the combined approach promising but says the next paradigm may not fit it and does not advocate realizing it before moving on.
